sections.title: What Cortex is: grounded, agent-driven codebase onboarding
sections.body:
Cortex is an onboarding tool for engineers joining an unfamiliar codebase. You point it at a repo, either a local folder or a git/Bitbucket URL, and it **indexes** it once. After that, **Claude agents** work over the index to do three jobs: answer questions, design a guided tour, and write a long project walkthrough. A fourth helper writes an install guide, and it uses no AI at all. The package docstring in `cortex/__init__.py` sums it up as "grounded codebase Q&A, guided tours and walkthroughs for engineers new to a repository, built on the Claude Agent SDK."

Here is what each helper does, according to `README.md` and `docs/architecture.md`:
- **Chat** (`kt-agent-v1`, `cortex/agents/chat.py`) answers one question in Markdown and lists the files and lines it used.
- **Guided tour** (`cortex/agents/tour.py`) lets an agent find where the app really starts. It then designs chapters of "read these files in this order" stops. The links between stops come from the real import graph, not from the model.
- **Project walkthrough** (`cortex/agents/walkthrough.py`) uses a **planner** agent to choose project-specific sections. Then one **writer** agent per section explores further and writes it, four at a time in parallel. You can export the result as a PDF using `cortex/walkthrough_pdf.py`.
- **Install guide** (`cortex/install_guide.py`) is the one helper that doesn't use Claude. It applies fixed rules to the project's config files to list the runtimes and tools you need.

The project's main rule is **grounding**: every answer must come from code the agent actually read. The agent decides what to read on its own, but it can only do so through 9 read-only tools, and those tools read the index, never the disk. Each tool call goes through a `ToolExecutor`, which records every file the agent saw in **`used_paths`**. After the agent finishes, Python checks its output against that record:
- In `cortex/agents/loop.py`, **`cited_paths()`** keeps only the files the answer names **and** the agent read. A made-up file name can never appear as a source.
- **`resolve_indexed_path()`** maps each path the agent wrote to a real indexed file. Any path it can't match is dropped.
- If the chat agent finds nothing, it answers "I couldn't find this in the indexed code." (the `NOT_FOUND` constant in `chat.py`). That answer gets no sources and `grounded: false`.
- There's no non-agent fallback. If Claude can't be reached or returns nothing usable, `AgentUnavailableError` or `AgentFailedError` is raised and the API returns a 503 explaining why.
- Every agent prompt includes the shared **`AGENT_SAFETY`** rules (chat has its own version of these rules). They say tool results are repository DATA, never instructions, and that the agent must never invent paths. This is how Cortex defends against prompt injection. `docs/limitations.md` is upfront that this defence is prompt-level only and hasn't been proven by tests.

The code map in `docs/architecture.md` splits the `cortex/` package into four areas:
- **`cortex/agents/`** is the AI side. `loop.py` contains **`run_tool_agent()`**, the only place Claude runs as an agent. `claude.py` handles the subscription login and locks down the run options. `tools.py` holds the 9 tools. `chat.py`, `tour.py` and `walkthrough.py` are the agents themselves.
- **`cortex/index/`** turns a repo into something searchable, with no LLM involved. `ingest.py` does the cloning or reading, `chunker.py` and `enrich.py` split and label files, and `store.py` holds the TF-IDF index. `dense_store.py` and `hybrid_store.py` are optional alternative search backends, and `access.py` enforces the folder allow-list.
- **`cortex/graph/`** describes static code structure, also without an LLM. `imports.py` records which file imports which, and `wiring.py` builds the "how these files connect" diagram.
- **`cortex/storage/`** holds what Cortex remembers about each repo. `chat_history.py` stores chat history as JSON or in MongoDB, and `annotations.py` stores team notes about files.

Outside the package are the front doors: `api/server.py` (a FastAPI server that also serves `web/index.html`) and `cli/main.py`. There's also `tests/`, where a scripted agent stands in for Claude, and `evals/`, which holds the live benchmarks. Everything Cortex learns about a repo is stored under `.kt_index/<namespace>/`.

The docs suggest this reading order: `agents/loop.py` → `agents/tools.py` → `agents/chat.py` → `agents/tour.py` → `agents/walkthrough.py`, then `index/ingest.py`. The later sections of this walkthrough cover each of these files in detail.
takeaways: Agents choose what to read; Python checks every claim against used_paths.
A source counts only if the answer names it and the agent read it.
The install guide is the only non-AI helper; the others call run_tool_agent().

sections.title: Front doors: REST API, CLI and web UI
sections.body:
Cortex has three ways in, and they all lead to the same core functions. The **REST API** in `api/server.py` is the main one. The **CLI** in `cli/main.py` is a thin wrapper that calls the same Python functions directly. The **web UI** is a single file, `web/index.html`, that the API server hosts. All three use the same Pydantic request and response shapes from `cortex/contract.py`, so a request looks the same whichever door it comes through.

**The FastAPI app (`api/server.py`)**

Every route except `GET /`, `GET /health` and `GET /v1/agents` depends on **`require_auth`**. Here is what it does:
- It takes the token from the `Authorization: Bearer ...` header and checks it against `settings.api_keys` using `hmac.compare_digest`. This constant-time comparison stops an attacker from guessing a key by timing the responses.
- It applies **`_rate_limit`** *before* it rejects a bad token, so people trying to brute-force keys are throttled too. The limiter keeps an in-memory sliding 60-second window per key. All invalid tokens share one `"anon"` bucket, and going over the limit returns **429**.
- If no keys are configured, every request is accepted ("open mode"). The `_warn_insecure_defaults` startup hook logs a loud warning when that happens. It also warns if the default `dev-local-key` is in use, or if `ONBOARDING_ALLOWED_ROOTS` is empty. In `cortex/config.py` the defaults are `ONBOARDING_API_KEYS=dev-local-key`, a 60 requests/minute limit and a 16 KB body cap (`ONBOARDING_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES`).

Routes that take a body read the raw bytes and pass them to **`_parse_body`**. It returns **413** if the body is larger than `max_request_bytes`. Otherwise it validates the body against a contract model, and any parse or validation failure becomes **422**. The slow work (ingesting, agent runs) is called through `run_in_threadpool`, so the event loop stays free while it runs.

The routes, grouped by purpose:
- **Ingest**: `POST /v1/ingest` calls `ingest_repo` with an `IngestRequest`. A per-repo lock (`_ingest_lock_for`) means two rebuilds of the *same* repo can't overlap their disk writes, while *different* repos still ingest in parallel. If the dense-search library (`fastembed`) is missing or the embedding model can't be loaded, you get a **503** instead of a crash. `POST /v1/resync/{namespace}` re-pulls an already-indexed repo through `resync_namespace`. It can take an optional `clone_token` for private repos.
- **Ask**: `POST /v1/ask` calls `cortex.agents.chat.ask` and returns an `AskResponse`. If the AI backend can't be built (for example a missing key or package), it returns **503**. `POST /v1/ask/stream` runs the same function on a background thread. That thread pushes progress events into a `Queue`, and an async generator sends them out as Server-Sent Events. A final event of type `done` carries the full `AskResponse`, and a `: ping` keep-alive line is sent when the stream is quiet.
- **Tour**: `GET /v1/tour/{namespace}` serves the cached `tour.json` if it was built by an agent and still validates. Otherwise it runs `build_tour` and *blocks until it finishes*, saves the result, then validates it against **`TourResponse`**. Add `?refresh=true` to force a rebuild. One quirk: the route has two `except RuntimeError` clauses, so only the first one runs. An agent failure therefore returns 400, not the 503 that the second clause intends.
- **Walkthrough**: `POST /v1/walkthrough/{namespace}` starts generation in the background with `fire_walkthrough_background`. `GET` is the one you poll, and it answers with `status` set to `generating`, `ready` (plus a `WalkthroughResponse`), `failed` or `absent`. `GET .../pdf` turns the cached walkthrough into a PDF with `build_walkthrough_pdf`.
- **Supporting data**: `GET /v1/file/{namespace}?path=...` rebuilds a file's full indexed text from its stored chunks (`store.full_file`). `GET`/`POST /v1/annotations/{namespace}` reads and saves team notes, using an `AnnotateRequest` for saves. `GET`/`DELETE /v1/chat/{namespace}` loads or clears the chat history. `GET /v1/namespaces` lists the indexed repos.
- **Agent catalog**: `GET /v1/agents` and `POST /v1/agents/{agent_id}/run` hand off to `cortex/install_guide.py`. An unknown `agent_id` returns 404.

Two **exception handlers** at the bottom of the file keep error responses consistent. Any `HTTPException` becomes `{"error": <detail>}`. Any other exception is logged with a new trace id and returns `{"error": "internal_error", "error_id": ...}`, so stack traces never reach the client.

**Contracts (`cortex/contract.py`)**

The request models (`IngestRequest`, `AskRequest`, `AnnotateRequest`) and most of the response models use `extra="forbid"`, so any unknown field is rejected. Note that `TourResponse` and `WalkthroughResponse` don't forbid extras. `AskRequest` is `namespace` + `question` + `history` (a list of `ChatTurn`s). `AskResponse` returns the `answer`, a list of `Source`s (each with `path`, line range, `snippet`, and a `used` flag marking whether the answer actually cited it), `grounded`, `wiring`, and a **`Trace`**. Every response carries a `Trace` with `trace_id`, `model_used`, `duration_ms`, `strategy` and an optional `grounding` block. The tour models nest as `TourResponse` → `TourChapter` → `TourStop`, and the walkthrough models as `WalkthroughResponse` → `WalkthroughSection` (with `body`, `takeaways` and `files`).

`docs/api.md` is a handy reference, but it is out of date in places. It shows errors under a `detail` key, while the code returns an `error` key. It also lists `top_k` and `backend` as fields you can send to `/v1/ask`, but because `AskRequest` forbids extra fields, those would actually be rejected with a 422.

**CLI (`cli/main.py`)**

The CLI is a small Typer app with four commands: `ingest` (`--repo`, `-n`, `--rebuild`), `ask "question" -n repo`, `namespaces` and `info`. It builds the same `IngestRequest`/`AskRequest` models and calls `ingest_repo` and `chat.ask` directly, with no HTTP and no auth. It prints the response as JSON and exits with code 2 on a `ValueError`. At startup it switches stdout and stderr to UTF-8 so Windows consoles don't crash on Unicode in code snippets. You run it with `python -m cli.main ...`.

**Web UI (`web/index.html`)**

`GET /` reads this one HTML file from disk and returns it with `no-store` cache headers, so edits show up on a plain refresh. The file is too large to quote here. `docs/api.md` says the `/v1/ask/stream` SSE endpoint exists so the UI can show live progress as the agent works. `docs/limitations.md` adds that the tour and walkthrough endpoints aren't streamed: the client keeps re-requesting until the result is ready.
takeaways: All routes share Pydantic contracts in cortex/contract.py; unknown request fields return 422.
require_auth checks the bearer token and rate-limits in memory; with no keys set, everything is open.
The CLI calls ingest_repo and chat.ask directly, with no HTTP and no auth.

sections.title: Ingest: turning a repo into a searchable index
sections.body:
Before any agent can answer a question, the repo has to become an **index**: a folder of chunks plus a search matrix that the agents' tools read later. Everything in this section starts at **`POST /v1/ingest`** in `api/server.py` and ends in files under `.kt_index/<namespace>/`.

**The endpoint.** In `api/server.py`, `ingest()` checks the bearer token, turns the body into an **`IngestRequest`** (a `repo_path` or a `clone_url`, plus an optional `clone_token`, `namespace` and `rebuild`), and calls `ingest_repo` from `cortex/index/ingest.py` on a worker thread. A lock is created for each repo, so two ingests of the same repo never write at the same time, while different repos can ingest side by side. Errors map to HTTP codes:
- `ValueError`, which includes `RepoAccessError`, returns 400.
- A missing `fastembed` package (`ImportError`) returns 503, with a hint to install it or switch to `tfidf`.
- A `RuntimeError` (for example, the embedding model can't download) returns 503.

**Step 1: pick a namespace before touching the repo.** `ingest_repo` first decides the namespace:
- For a clone URL, `_namespace_from_clone_url` takes the repo name from the URL (`.../my-repo.git` → `my-repo`). The clone lands in a temp folder literally named `repo`, so the folder name is useless.
- For a local path, it uses the folder's name. `_clean_path` first strips the quotes that Windows "Copy as path" adds.
- Either way, `slugify` in `cortex/index/store.py` cleans the name.

If `store.exists(namespace)` is true and `rebuild` is false, `_cached_ingest_response` returns at once with `already_indexed=True`. No clone, no re-index. The code calls this the "track record".

**Step 2: get the source.** For a URL, `_clone_repo` runs `git clone --depth=1 --single-branch` into a temp folder (`cortex_clone_*`), with a 5-minute timeout. Auth works three ways:
- **With a token:** it's sent as a Basic `http.extraHeader`, built by `_build_auth_header`. Both `user:token` and a bare token work; a bare token gets the user `x-token-auth` (Bitbucket) or `x-access-token`.
- **No token, `ONBOARDING_CLONE_INTERACTIVE` true (the default):** Git can try its normal credential prompt.
- **No token, headless:** prompts are turned off and the timeout drops to 60s, so a private repo fails fast instead of hanging.

The temp folder is deleted on every exit path, success or failure.

**Step 3: the folder check.** `_check_allowed` in `cortex/index/access.py` runs **before anything is written**. It resolves the path and requires it to sit under one of the comma-separated `ONBOARDING_ALLOWED_ROOTS` (read in `cortex/config.py`). Otherwise it raises `RepoAccessError`. If the variable is empty, any path is allowed, and the server's startup hook logs a loud "FS UNRESTRICTED" warning. Watch out: for clones, the check runs against the temp clone folder.

**Step 4: chunking at symbol boundaries.** `iter_chunks` in `cortex/index/chunker.py` walks the repo and decides what to read:
- It skips heavy or noisy folders (`.git`, `node_modules`, `dist`, `.kt_index`, …), lock and minified files, and binaries. It also skips any copy of Cortex found inside the repo, because Cortex's own prompts would hijack search results.
- It keeps only known text extensions, caps the number of files (`ONBOARDING_MAX_INGEST_FILES`, default 4000), and caps bytes per file (`ONBOARDING_MAX_INGEST_FILE_BYTES`, default 60000).

`_slice` then cuts each file into chunks:
- Per-language regexes mark where a new unit starts: Python `def`/`class`/decorators, C-like `function`/`class`/`fn`/`func`/`const x =`, Ruby `def`, Markdown headings. Files without a pattern split at paragraphs.
- Whole units are packed together up to `ONBOARDING_CHUNK_CHARS` (default 1200). A unit too big for that is cut into line-aligned windows with overlap (`ONBOARDING_CHUNK_OVERLAP`, default 150).

Each chunk has:
- an `id` (`path#n`)
- `text`: the exact file content, used for display and citations
- `index_text`: the path plus the text, which is what gets searched
- `metadata`: path, language, `symbol`, `line_start`/`line_end`

If no chunks come out, `_explain_empty` says why (empty folder, only skipped folders, or a wrapper around a Cortex copy).

**Step 5: i18n labels and git commits.** `cortex/index/enrich.py` adds business context without an LLM:
- **i18n labels:** `build_i18n_labels` reads English/default translation JSON (in `i18n`/`locale`/`lang` folders, or files like `en.json`) into a key → label map. `enrich_chunks` then appends `UI labels: ...` to the `index_text` of any chunk that uses one of those keys. Only `index_text` changes, so citations stay exact.
- **Commits:** `build_commit_chunks` runs `git log` (up to `ONBOARDING_MAX_COMMIT_CHUNKS`, default 100, no merges) and turns each commit into its own chunk. The path is `git-history`, the id is `git-history#<hash>`, and the text holds the date, author, message and changed files. The code says commit messages are deliberately *not* added to code chunks, because that changed their text on every re-sync and broke the dense embedding cache.

**Step 6: write `.kt_index/<namespace>`.** `store.index(namespace, chunks, meta)` writes the index under `ONBOARDING_INDEX_DIR` (default `.kt_index`). Every backend writes `chunks.json` and `meta.json`; meta includes `repo_path`, `n_files`, `clone_url`, `indexed_at` and `backend`. The base `VectorStore` reads `chunks.json` back to rebuild whole files (`full_file`), run regex search (`grep_chunks`) and list `known_paths`. Afterwards, `ingest_repo` writes a trace record and returns an **`IngestResponse`** with file and chunk counts.

`resync_namespace` (behind `POST /v1/resync/{namespace}`) re-runs the same pipeline on a background thread with `rebuild=True`. It reads the original `clone_url` or `repo_path` from `meta.json`, and repeated clicks merge into one job.

**Choosing a search backend.** `get_store` picks the backend from `ONBOARDING_VECTOR_BACKEND` and keeps one store per backend and index folder, so the index isn't reloaded on every request. All three backends over-fetch candidates and then call the same `rerank`. `rerank` boosts files whose name matches the query and halves test/spec files unless the question is about tests. It also multiplies `git-history` chunks by 0.25, or by 1.3 when the question is about history.
- **`tfidf` (default), `TfidfStore` in `cortex/index/store.py`:** fully offline. It uses scikit-learn `TfidfVectorizer` with `split_identifiers`, which splits camelCase and snake_case so "rate limiting" matches `rate_limit`. It uses 1–2-word ngrams, saves `tfidf.joblib`, and ranks by cosine similarity. It's fast and good at exact identifiers.
- **`dense`, `DenseStore` in `cortex/index/dense_store.py`:** embeds `index_text` with fastembed (`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` by default, run locally on CPU) and saves `dense.npy` plus `dense_keys.json`. It catches meaning (a question about "authentication" can find `login`). Re-indexing is **incremental**: chunks with the same id and text hash reuse their old vectors. It's slower to ingest and needs `fastembed`.
- **`hybrid`, `HybridStore` in `cortex/index/hybrid_store.py`:** builds both indexes and merges the two result lists with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion** (`rrf_merge`, K=60), so chunks both methods agree on rise to the top. It builds the dense index first, because dense reuse needs the old `chunks.json` that TF-IDF overwrites. Above `ONBOARDING_HYBRID_MAX_CHUNKS` (default 4000) it skips dense, deletes stale dense files and works as TF-IDF only. It records `backend: hybrid` and `dense: true/false` in meta.

Each backend's `exists()` checks for its own files. A namespace built with one backend looks "not indexed" to another, so `/v1/ingest` will rebuild it after you switch backends.
takeaways: Ingest reuses an existing index unless rebuild=true; check ONBOARDING_ALLOWED_ROOTS before writing.
Chunks: text is the exact source for citations; only index_text is enriched and searched.
Use tfidf (fast, offline) by default; dense finds meaning; hybrid merges both with RRF.

sections.title: The agent core: run_tool_agent and the Claude connection
sections.body:
Every AI feature in Cortex goes through one function: **`run_tool_agent`** in `cortex/agents/loop.py`. The chat agent (`chat.py`), the guided tour (`tour.py`) and the walkthrough planner and writers (`walkthrough.py`) all call it. Each passes in its own system prompt, user prompt and turn limit. Anything that changes how Claude runs, such as login, tools or error handling, changes in this file and in `cortex/agents/claude.py`, which handles the connection.

**How a run works.** Cortex uses the Claude Agent SDK (`claude-agent-sdk`). The docstring in `cortex/agents/claude.py` explains that the SDK starts the bundled Claude Code CLI as a subprocess, and that CLI runs the tool-use loop. Python never decides what to read. Claude picks a tool, and Python runs that call and returns the result. `run_tool_agent` does this:
- It calls **`get_claude(settings)`** to get a `ClaudeConnection`. This step checks the login rules.
- It builds the in-process MCP server and the list of allowed tool names.
- It calls the SDK's `query(prompt, options)` and reads the stream of messages. When an `AssistantMessage` contains a `ToolUseBlock`, the turn counter goes up and an `iteration` event goes to the optional `event_callback`. The latest text is kept as a fallback answer. When the `ResultMessage` arrives, its `result` becomes the final answer.
- It returns `(final_text, tool_turns)`. The callback also gets `thinking` at the start and `composing` at the end, which the UI uses to show live progress.

Errors reported by the SDK are not raised. If an `AssistantMessage` has `msg.error` set (for example a rate limit or billing problem), the loop adds `sdk_error:...` to the caller's `errors` list and **breaks**. A code comment explains why it breaks instead of raising: raising inside the stream makes the SDK's async generator crash when it closes. If a `ResultMessage` reports an error, `sdk_result_error:...` is recorded the same way.

**The tools as the in-process 'kt' MCP server.** `_build_mcp_server` calls `create_sdk_mcp_server(name="kt", ...)` with the tools produced by `_make_sdk_tools`:
- `_make_sdk_tools` wraps every entry in **`TOOL_DEFINITIONS`** using the SDK's `tool(name, description, input_schema)` decorator, keeping the original JSON schema.
- Each handler sends a `tool_call` event, runs **`executor.execute(name, args)`** on the shared `ToolExecutor`, sends a `tool_result` event with `ok` and a character count, and returns the output as MCP text content.

Because every call goes through the executor, the executor records which files the agent actually read. That record is what the grounding checks rely on later. Claude sees the tools as `mcp__kt__search_code` and so on, while the prompts use the short names. **`TOOLS_NOTE`** is appended to every system prompt to explain the naming and to tell Claude it has no other tools. `tests/test_claude_connection.py` (`test_make_sdk_tools_covers_all_definitions_and_routes`) checks that every definition is wrapped, its schema is kept, and each handler routes to the executor and emits both events.

**How the run is locked down.** `ClaudeConnection.base_options()` builds the `ClaudeAgentOptions` that every run starts from:
- `tools=[]` turns off all of Claude Code's built-in tools (Read, Bash and so on).
- `setting_sources=None` makes the CLI ignore any `CLAUDE.md` or local settings files.
- `allowed_tools=[]` by default. `run_tool_agent` overrides it with exactly the `mcp__kt__<name>` tools.
- `permission_mode="bypassPermissions"`. A code comment explains this is safe because only Cortex's own read-only tools can run.
- `model` is `CLAUDE_SDK_MODEL`. If that is empty, the subscription's default model is used.
- `env` carries the login environment worked out below.

The connection also has `complete()`, a single question and answer with no tools and retries with backoff. Its docstring says the app itself does not use it; only the live RAGAS benchmark uses it, as its judge.

**Subscription OAuth only; `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is refused.** `ClaudeConnection.__init__` calls **`resolve_subscription_auth`** right away, so a bad login fails immediately:
- If `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set, it raises a `RuntimeError`, unless `ONBOARDING_CLAUDE_SDK_ALLOW_API_KEY` is set to an opt-in value. The docstring gives the reason: the CLI prefers an API key over OAuth, so a stray key would quietly bill the API.
- If there is no OAuth token (from `Settings.claude_sdk_oauth_token` or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`) and no `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, it raises an error telling you to run `claude setup-token` or log in once with `claude`.
- If a token exists, it is passed to the CLI subprocess as `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`.

The comments in `cortex/config.py` describe the same rules. The tests in `tests/test_claude_connection.py` check that a billed key is refused and that a token is passed through.

A related helper is `cortex/_tls.py`, which `cortex/__init__.py` imports so it runs when the package loads. It injects `truststore` so Python's HTTPS checks use the operating system's certificate store. Its docstring says this is for corporate proxies that re-sign traffic with an internal certificate. You can turn it off with `ONBOARDING_DISABLE_TRUSTSTORE=1`.

**The two error types.** Both are defined in `cortex/agents/loop.py`:
- **`AgentUnavailableError`**: Claude can't be used at all, for example no login, an API key that isn't allowed, or the SDK isn't installed. `run_tool_agent` raises it by converting any `RuntimeError` or `ImportError` from `get_claude`. It is never retried. In `cortex/agents/tour.py` the retry loop re-raises it straight away and retries any other exception once.
- **`AgentFailedError`**: the agent ran but its output can't be used, for example the JSON is invalid or every path it named was made up. The run itself never raises this. The callers raise it after checking the result. For example, `tour.py` raises it when `_validate_tour_spec` returns `None`.

The docstrings say the API turns both into a 503 that includes the reason.

**`run_sync` threading.** The SDK is async but the rest of the app is synchronous. **`run_sync(coro_factory)`** in `cortex/agents/claude.py` starts a new daemon thread. That thread calls `asyncio.run(coro_factory())` with its own event loop, and the calling thread waits for it with `join()`. Any exception is caught in the worker thread and raised again on the caller's thread. You pass a zero-argument function that builds the coroutine, not the coroutine itself, so the coroutine is created inside the worker thread. Because each run gets a fresh thread and loop, it works even if the calling thread already has an event loop running. `run_tool_agent` ends with `return run_sync(_run)`.
takeaways: Every agent goes through run_tool_agent; the only tools it gets are mcp__kt__*.
Built-in tools and local settings are off; a set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY stops the run.
AgentUnavailableError is never retried; callers raise AgentFailedError for unusable output.

sections.title: The 9 read-only tools and how grounding is tracked
sections.body:
Every agent in Cortex has the same nine tools, and they are its only way to see the code. They are defined in `cortex/agents/tools.py`. There are two parts. **TOOL_DEFINITIONS** is a list of tool schemas written in Claude's format. **ToolExecutor** is the class that actually runs each call. `cortex/agents/loop.py` wraps each tool as an in-process MCP tool and serves them from a server named **kt**. That's why Claude sees them as `mcp__kt__search_code` and so on. Each handler just calls `executor.execute(tool_name, args)`. Python never decides what to read: it only runs the calls Claude asks for. **TOOLS_NOTE** is appended to every system prompt and tells Claude it has no other tools, so it can't read the filesystem or run commands.

None of the tools touch the repo on disk. Every one of them reads the ingested index through the **VectorStore** in `cortex/index/store.py`. That store loads the namespace's saved `chunks.json` and caches it by file modification time. The tools use these store methods:
- **search** does a TF-IDF cosine search. It fetches extra results, then reranks them with `rerank`. That boosts files whose names match the query and lowers the scores of test files and the `git-history` entry, unless the question asks for them.
- **full_file** rebuilds a whole file by joining its chunks back together in order. It flags `truncated` if the file hit the ingest size limit.
- **known_paths** returns every indexed path.
- **grep_chunks** runs a case-insensitive regex over the chunk text and stops after 25 matching chunks.

A file that was never indexed doesn't exist as far as the agent is concerned.

Here are the nine tools:
- **search_code**: ranked search over chunks (`top_k` defaults to 8, max 20). Returns `[path:start-end]` snippets with relevance scores.
- **read_file**: the full indexed file from `full_file`. If the exact path isn't found, it falls back to the shortest indexed path that contains the given string, so `tools.py` works.
- **find_files**: substring or glob match against `known_paths`. Returns up to 80 paths.
- **get_file_structure**: lists every indexed path (up to 400).
- **grep_code**: regex search through `grep_chunks`, showing only the matching lines from each chunk. The optional `file_glob` is applied *after* the 25-chunk cap. A pattern that's common elsewhere can therefore return nothing for your glob even when the file contains it.
- **list_symbols**: runs the per-language regexes in `_SYM_RULES` (TS/JS, Python, Go, Java/Kotlin, Rust) over one file. Returns the file's symbols and line numbers without the file body.
- **get_dependencies**: finds manifest files such as `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod` and `Cargo.toml` (it reads up to four) and parses them with `_parse_dep_file`.
- **call_graph**: built from regex searches, not real parsing. It finds the definition with grep, lists the places that call the name with a `\bname\s*\(` pattern, and guesses what it calls with `_extract_callees`, which scans the first 3,000 characters of the body.
- **run_grep_ast**: despite the name, it doesn't parse an AST. It applies the regex groups in `_AST_PATTERNS` for class, function, interface, component, decorator, route or export, and returns up to 50 hits.

`execute` catches any exception and returns it as a `Tool error (...)` string, so a bad call never crashes the agent loop. The loop's handler treats that prefix as a failed call in the UI's progress events.

Grounding is tracked by two attributes on ToolExecutor:
- **call_log** records every tool name and its input.
- **used_paths** is a set of every file path a tool *showed* to Claude. That covers search hits, files that were read, grep hits, symbol listings, dependency manifests, `call_graph` definitions and call sites, and `run_grep_ast` matches.

`find_files` and `get_file_structure` list paths but don't add them. Seeing a filename doesn't count as reading the file.

Every check on what an agent returns compares against `used_paths`. The helpers are in `cortex/agents/loop.py`:
- **resolve_indexed_path** maps a path the model wrote to a real indexed path. It accepts an exact match or a single unique suffix match, and returns nothing for anything else, which drops invented paths.
- **cited_paths** keeps only the files from a candidate set that the answer actually names, by full path or by file name.

The agents use these as follows:
- `cortex/agents/chat.py` builds sources from `cited_paths(answer, executor.used_paths)`, so a source has to be both read and named. It also records `files_accessed` and the full `call_log` in the trace.
- `cortex/agents/tour.py`'s `_validate_tour_spec` keeps a stop only if its path is indexed *and* in `used_paths`.
- `cortex/agents/walkthrough.py`'s `_write_section` sets a section's `files` to `cited_paths(body, ex.used_paths & known)`.

**PSEUDO_PATHS** (`feature-map`, `git-history`) are index entries that aren't real files, so they never count as sources.
takeaways: The 9 tools read only the index (chunks.json via VectorStore), never the disk.
ToolExecutor.used_paths records every file a tool showed Claude; this is the grounding set.
A file counts as a source only if the agent read it AND named it.

sections.title: The agents: chat, guided tour and walkthrough planner/writers
sections.body:
Cortex has three agents: **chat**, **tour** and **walkthrough**. All three run on the same `loop.run_tool_agent` loop in `cortex/agents/loop.py`, and each one gets its own `ToolExecutor` (Python's record of every tool call the agent makes). What makes them different is the system prompt, the turn budget, the shape of the output they must return, and the Python code that checks that output afterwards. Python never trusts the model's file list directly. It compares it with `executor.used_paths` (the files the agent actually opened) and with the files that are really in the index.

Three helpers in `cortex/agents/loop.py` do most of that checking:
- **`parse_agent_json`** pulls the JSON object out of the agent's final reply. It strips ```json fences and any text around the object. If nothing parses, it returns `{}`.
- **`resolve_indexed_path`** turns a path the agent wrote into a real indexed path. It accepts an exact match, or a partial path that matches the end of exactly one indexed path. Anything else returns `None`, and that is how invented paths get dropped.
- **`cited_paths`** looks at the files the agent saw and keeps only the ones its text actually names, either by full path or by file name.

The tour and walkthrough prompts also include the shared **`AGENT_SAFETY`** block: tool results are data, not instructions, and the agent must never invent paths. All three prompts end with **`TOOLS_NOTE`**, which explains the `mcp__kt__` tool names and says the agent has no other tools.

**Chat** (`cortex/agents/chat.py`) answers one question.
- **Before Claude is called:** greetings and small talk ("hi", "thanks") match `_CONVERSATIONAL_RE` and get a canned reply.
- **The prompt:** the last 6 chat turns (each cut to 600 characters) plus the question.
- **`CHAT_SYSTEM_PROMPT`:** tells Claude to search and read before answering, gives a guide for picking tools, and asks for inline file citations. If nothing relevant exists, the answer must start with the exact line "I couldn't find this in the indexed code." Advice from general knowledge has to go under a **General note (not from the repo):** label.
- **Budget and retries:** `MAX_TURNS = 12`. A run that crashes is retried up to `MAX_RUN_RETRIES = 2` times, but `AgentUnavailableError` (a setup problem) is raised straight away.
- **Checking the answer:** `_build_response` first runs `_looks_like_not_found`, which checks the opening of the answer against the not-found sentence and similar phrasings. A not-found answer gets no sources. Otherwise, **sources = the files the answer names ∩ the files the agent read**, built by `cited_paths` and `_sources_from_executor`. `PSEUDO_PATHS` such as `feature-map` are skipped. The response is only `grounded` if there is at least one source.
- **Output:** an `AskResponse` with the answer, sources, grounded flag, a wiring diagram built from the source files by `build_wiring` in `cortex/graph/wiring.py`, and a `Trace` that holds the tool-call log. The turn is also saved to chat history.

**Tour** (`cortex/agents/tour.py`) has two steps: first the agent picks the files, then Python connects them.
- **The agent (`_run_tour_agent`):** gets `TOUR_MAX_TURNS = 30` and one retry. `TOUR_SYSTEM_PROMPT` tells it to orient itself, confirm the real entry point by reading it, and design chapters in the project's own vocabulary. It may only include a file as a stop if it opened it. It must return JSON with `overview`, `entry_point`, and `chapters[].stops[]`, where each stop has `path`, `reason` and `insight`. `_tour_prompt` asks for roughly one stop per 7 source files, kept between the configured minimum and maximum (`tour_min_stops` / `tour_max_stops`).
- **Checking the tour (`_validate_tour_spec`):** a stop survives only if its path resolves to an indexed file **and** the agent saw it (it is in `executor.used_paths`). Duplicate stops are dropped and text fields are trimmed. Fewer than 2 surviving stops means the tour is unusable, and `AgentFailedError` is raised. If the entry point the agent named didn't survive, the first stop takes its place.
- **Connecting the stops (`_assemble_tour`):** nothing in this step comes from the model. `build_import_graph` in `cortex/graph/imports.py` scans every source file's import statements to build the import graph (who imports whom). `bfs_depth` gives each stop its distance from the entry point. Each stop's `connections` list shows which other stops it **uses** and which stops it is **used_by**, labelled with the real names imported across that link. Python also builds the `flow_graph` mini-map and a `build_wiring` diagram. The result is cached to `tour.json`, because a run takes about a minute.

**Walkthrough** (`cortex/agents/walkthrough.py`) uses a planner/writer pattern: one planner agent designs the outline, then writer agents fill in the sections.
- **The planner (`_plan`):** gets `PLANNER_MAX_TURNS = 30` and one retry. `PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT` asks for 5–10 sections that fit this specific project. It should start with an overview and end with build/run if the repo shows how. Each section lists 2–8 files the planner saw. The output is `{stack, sections[{key, title, goal, files}]}`.
- **Checking the plan (`_validate_outline`):** keeps at most 12 sections, makes keys unique, and passes every file through `resolve_indexed_path`, so invented paths are dropped. Fewer than 3 valid sections raises `AgentFailedError`.
- **The writers (`_write_section`):** one per section, run 4 at a time by a `ThreadPoolExecutor` (`_WRITER_WORKERS = 4`), each with `WRITER_MAX_TURNS = 14`. The first wave starts 2 seconds apart (`_WRITER_STAGGER_S`), because simultaneous Claude CLI launches can collide on `~/.claude.json`. `_writer_prompt` gives each writer the full outline, its own section's goal and its suggested files. A writer returns `{explanation, takeaways}`. If one writer fails, its section gets a placeholder body and the other sections are unaffected.
- **Checking each section:** a section's `files` are the files the writer both opened **and** named in its text. If that list is empty, Python falls back to the suggested files the writer opened, then to the plain suggestions.
- **Running and saving it:** `fire_walkthrough_background` runs the whole job on a daemon thread. The finished document is saved to `walkthrough.json`. If the run fails, the error is stored in `_WALK_ERRORS` so the API can report it.

Finally, `cortex/walkthrough_pdf.py` (`build_walkthrough_pdf`) turns the finished walkthrough into a PDF with reportlab. For each section it shows the title, the takeaways, the body (a small subset of Markdown: bold, code and bullets) and the files list.
takeaways: Python checks every agent's file list against the index and against files the agent actually opened.
Chat sources are files the answer names that the agent also read.
Tour links come from the static import graph; walkthrough writers run 4 at a time.

sections.title: Non-AI helpers, persistence and tracing
sections.body:
Not everything in Cortex goes through Claude. This section covers three supporting pieces. One is a small **rule-based install guide**. Another is **per-repo memory**, which holds chat history and team notes. The last is an **observability layer** that lets you follow any request through logs and a trace file.

**The install guide (no LLM)**

`cortex/install_guide.py` answers "what do I install, and how do I run this?" using fixed rules, not an agent. Its own docstring says it is the only helper that is not an agent. The flow:
- **`read_repo_setup_files`** finds the repo's README and a fixed list of root config files, such as `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, `Dockerfile`, `go.mod` and `.env.example`. It keeps only the first 6 KB of each.
- **`install_guide`** first calls `_check_allowed` (from `cortex/index/access.py`), so the same allowed-roots safety check applies here. Then it applies two tables:
  - **`_SETUP_RULES`** maps a config filename to setup steps. For example, `requirements.txt` gives "Create a virtualenv" and "pip install -r requirements.txt".
  - **`_PREREQ`** runs regexes over the config contents, the README and the config file names. Each match adds a toolchain requirement, such as "Python 3.9+" for fastapi/flask/django or "Docker Desktop" for docker/compose.
- When nothing matches, the result says so: setup steps become `"not found in repo"`, and prerequisites fall back to a generic "check the README" line.

The guide is registered in a tiny **`HELPERS`** registry built from `HelperSpec` entries. `list_agents` and `run_agent` expose that registry. In `api/server.py`, they back `GET /v1/agents` and `POST /v1/agents/{id}/run`. That route checks the request size and requires `repo_path`. It runs the scan in a threadpool. An unknown id returns 404, and a `ValueError` returns 400.

**Chat history: one interface, two backends**

`cortex/storage/chat_history.py` stores each repo's (namespace's) conversation.
- **`JsonChatStore`** is the default and needs no setup. It writes one `chat_history.json` inside the namespace's index directory.
- **`MongoChatStore`** keeps one document per namespace. It appends with a single `$push` + `$slice` update, so the cap is applied atomically and concurrent questions can't corrupt the list.
- Both store turns shaped like `{role, content, ts}`. They keep at most **80 turns** and trim questions to 2000 characters and answers to 4000. An assistant turn can carry extra data. `cortex/agents/chat.py` uses this to save the answer's `sources` and `wiring` diagram, so a refreshed UI can show exactly what was on screen before.
- **`get_chat_store`** picks the backend from `ONBOARDING_CHAT_STORE` in `cortex/config.py`. The values are `auto` (the default), `mongo` or `json`. In `auto` or `mongo` mode it tries Mongo only if `ONBOARDING_MONGO_URI` is set, `pymongo` can be imported, and a ping succeeds within 2 seconds. Otherwise it quietly falls back to JSON and logs the reason. The chosen store is cached per settings combination, so it doesn't reconnect on every call.

The chat agent calls `get_chat_store(...).append(...)` inside a `try/except` at the end of `_build_response`. A storage failure never breaks an answer. The API exposes `GET /v1/chat/{ns}` and `DELETE /v1/chat/{ns}` through `load_chat_history` and `clear_chat_history`.

**Team annotations**

`cortex/storage/annotations.py` stores short human notes about a file or symbol in `annotations.json` under the namespace directory.
- **`save_annotation`** works like an upsert keyed on `(file, symbol)`. Any old note for that pair is replaced, answers are capped at 1500 characters, and an empty answer deletes the note. `tests/test_engine.py` covers that delete behaviour.
- The API exposes `GET` and `POST /v1/annotations/{ns}`.
- `cortex/agents/tour.py` calls **`load_annotations`** while building the guided tour. The module docstring says the notes show up as the matching tour stop's `note`.

**Observability: trace IDs, JSON logs and trace.json**

`cortex/trace.py` is small, but every agent run goes through it.
- **`logger`** is the `"cortex"` logger. It writes one JSON object per line to stderr with `ts`, `level`, `msg`, and, when present, `trace_id` and `event`. The level comes from `ONBOARDING_LOG_LEVEL`.
- **`new_trace_id`** creates IDs like `tr_<16 hex chars>`. **`log_event(event, trace_id)`** writes start and end markers. For example, `chat.py` logs `chat_ask_start` and `chat_ask_end`, and `cortex/index/ingest.py` logs `ingest_start` and `ingest_end`.
- **`timed()`** is a context manager that puts the elapsed milliseconds into `holder["ms"]`. That value becomes `duration_ms`.
- **`append_trace`** adds one JSON line per run to `ONBOARDING_TRACE_FILE` (default `trace.json`, see `.env.example`). Despite the `.json` name, the file is newline-delimited JSON. Chat writes an `agent_ask` entry with question, tool-call count, files accessed, iterations and duration. Ingest writes an `ingest` entry. A write failure is only logged as a warning, so tracing can never crash the agent.
- The same `trace_id` is returned to the caller in the response's `Trace` object, along with the full tool `call_log`. That one ID links the API response, the stderr logs and the `trace.json` entry. `api/server.py` uses `new_trace_id` too: its catch-all exception handler returns an `error_id` with every 500 and logs the same ID, so a user's bug report can be matched to the log line.
takeaways: Install guide is pure rules over README/config files — no Claude call.
Chat history defaults to JSON; Mongo is used only if reachable, else silently falls back.
One trace_id ties together the response, stderr JSON logs and trace.json lines.

sections.title: Testing with a scripted agent, and live evals
sections.body:
Cortex is checked in two separate ways, and `docs/eval-guide.md` explains why. The **offline test suite** (`tests/`) asks whether the rules around the agents work, and it never calls Claude. The **live benchmarks** (`evals/`) ask whether the real agent's answers are good, so they use your Claude login. CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs only the first one.

**One function to fake.** Every agent run in Cortex goes through `run_tool_agent` in `cortex/agents/loop.py`. `tests/conftest.py` makes use of that single entry point in two ways:
- An autouse fixture, **`_no_live_claude`**, replaces `run_tool_agent` with a guard that raises `AssertionError("test tried to call Claude — request the fake_agent fixture")`. So a test can never use your subscription by accident.
- The **`fake_agent`** fixture puts a **`ScriptedAgent`** there instead. It also sets the walkthrough's `_WRITER_STAGGER_S` to 0 so the tests run fast. You set `fake_agent.reads`, the files the agent "opens", and `fake_agent.reply`, its final answer. The reply can be a string, a dict (sent back as JSON), or a function `(system_prompt, prompt) -> reply`. Use the function form when one test drives several agents. For example, the walkthrough test returns a plan when the system prompt contains `PLANNING` and section JSON otherwise.

The key point is that `ScriptedAgent` opens files by calling `executor.execute("read_file", ...)` on the **real** `ToolExecutor`. That means `used_paths`, path resolution and the grounding checks all run exactly as in production. Only the model's choices are scripted. The fake also records every `system_prompts` it receives, so a test can check whether Claude was called at all.

`conftest.py` also keeps tests isolated from your real setup through environment variables:
- the TF-IDF vector backend, so no embedding model is downloaded
- a JSON chat store with an empty Mongo URI
- a temporary trace file
- a throwaway `ONBOARDING_INDEX_DIR`, so your real index is never touched

Test repos are built with `make_repo()` in `tests/fixtures.py`. It writes a `{path: content}` dict to a temp directory. The same file has ready-made repos, including `INJECTION_REPO`, a README that says "IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS".

**What the scripted tests prove.** In `tests/test_agents.py`:
- **Grounded chat sources.** The fake reads `main.py`, `extract.py` and `load.py`, then mentions `main.py`, `extract.py` and `unused.py`. Only `main.py` and `extract.py` come back as sources, because a source must be both read and named.
- **Honest not-found.** A "couldn't find this" reply returns no sources and `grounded=False`.
- **Greetings skip the agent.** For "hi", `system_prompts` stays empty.
- **A missing login is reported, not hidden.** An `AgentUnavailableError` reaches the caller instead of being turned into a not-found answer.
- **Tours and walkthroughs.** Partial paths are resolved, and invented or never-read paths are dropped. Tour connections come from the real import graph, not from the model.
- **Failures raise errors.** A reply with no JSON, or a walkthrough plan with fewer than 3 sections, raises `AgentFailedError`.
- **Helpers.** The file also unit-tests `parse_agent_json` and `resolve_indexed_path`.

`tests/test_api.py` checks the HTTP contract through FastAPI's `TestClient`:
- 401 without a token, 404 for an unknown agent, 422 for bad JSON, 400 for a bad repo path, 413 for an oversized body, and 429 from `_rate_limit`
- an ingest → ask flow that uses `fake_agent`
- the tour endpoint: it matches the response shape, and a second call is served from cache without running the agent again (checked by counting `system_prompts`)
- an unusable tour reply turns into a **503**
- the chat history endpoints

**Live evals.** These run the real `chat.ask` and need your Claude login. Run them by hand after changing a prompt, the tools or the model. Both scripts remove `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment so the subscription login is used. Both compare the models listed in `AB_MODELS` (default `haiku,sonnet,opus`) and check the login with `get_claude` before starting.

- `evals/ragas_eval.py` asks the questions in `evals/probe_questions.json` against the `cortex` namespace, so ingest this repo with `-n cortex` first. For each cited source it pulls the full file content, then has an LLM judge (`AB_JUDGE_MODEL`, default `sonnet`) score **faithfulness**, **answer_relevancy** and **context_relevance** from 0 to 1. The last probe, about Stripe payments, is a negative control. It is scored as **abstention**: the answer passes only if it is ungrounded and has no sources. Results go to `evals/ragas_results.json`.
- `evals/repoqa_eval.py` downloads the public RepoQA dataset and caches it in `evals/.cache/`. It writes each sampled repo to a temp directory, ingests it with `ingest_repo`, and asks the agent to find each "needle" function from its description. A needle counts as **located** only if the answer names the function and the right file shows up in the answer or the sources. If the agent hits a rate limit, it retries with backoff. Results go to `evals/repoqa_results.json`. The docstring warns that the scores are only loosely comparable to the RepoQA leaderboard, because this tests Cortex's retrieval rather than long-context recall.
takeaways: Tests patch loop.run_tool_agent; use fake_agent, or the guard fails the test.
The scripted agent reads through the real ToolExecutor, so grounding rules are really tested.
RAGAS and RepoQA evals call Claude for real, run by hand, not in CI.

sections.title: Setting up, authenticating and running Cortex
sections.body:
Cortex is a plain Python app, so setup is short: create a virtualenv, install the requirements, log in to Claude once, then start one Uvicorn process. That process serves the web UI and the REST API together. The `README.md` "Get it running" section is the source for these steps. The code that enforces the rules is in `cortex/config.py` and `cortex/agents/claude.py`.

**1. Virtualenv and dependencies.** The only hard requirements are Python and the Claude Code CLI. The CLI is needed only for the one-time login. From the project folder:

- `python -m venv .venv`
- `.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt`

`requirements.txt` groups the packages by role:

- **Agent runtime:** `claude-agent-sdk` is the only LLM backend and bundles the Claude Code CLI. `httpx` and `truststore` handle networking.
- **Search index:** `scikit-learn` and `numpy` for TF-IDF, plus `fastembed` for optional dense embeddings.
- **Access layer:** `fastapi`, `uvicorn[standard]` and `typer`, plus `reportlab` for walkthrough PDFs.
- **Tests:** `pytest`.

MongoDB is optional. Without it, chat history goes to local JSON files.

**2. One-time Claude login.** Cortex has no API key of its own. It runs on your Claude Pro/Max subscription over OAuth. Run `claude setup-token`, or just `claude` for an interactive login. Claude Code, not Cortex, saves the credentials under `~/.claude`. If you use `setup-token`, copy the long-lived token it prints into **`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`**. That method suits servers and CI.

The check happens in **`resolve_subscription_auth()`** in `cortex/agents/claude.py`. It runs every time **`ClaudeConnection`** is built, so a bad login fails fast:

- If **`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`** is set, it raises a `RuntimeError`. The reason: the CLI prefers that key over OAuth, which would silently bill the metered API. The only way past this is **`ONBOARDING_CLAUDE_SDK_ALLOW_API_KEY=1`**, which you'd set only if you mean to use a key. So keep `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` unset.
- If there is no `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` and no `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, it raises an error telling you to run `claude setup-token` or `claude`.
- If a token is set, it is passed explicitly into the env of the CLI subprocess.

The live eval scripts `evals/ragas_eval.py` and `evals/repoqa_eval.py` remove `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment for the same reason.

**3. Start the app.** Run `.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m uvicorn api.server:app --port 8000` and open http://localhost:8000. Interactive API docs are at `/docs`.

`api/server.py` builds the FastAPI `app` and serves the UI from the `web/` folder. At startup, **`_warn_insecure_defaults()`** logs warnings when:

- the API key list is empty (the API is open to everyone),
- the default `dev-local-key` is still in use,
- `ONBOARDING_ALLOWED_ROOTS` is blank (any local path can be ingested).

These defaults are fine on your laptop. Fix them before sharing the server.

**Configuration.** `cortex/config.py` defines a frozen **`Settings`** dataclass. It calls `load_dotenv()`, so you can copy `.env.example` to `.env` instead of exporting variables. Each field reads its environment variable when settings are built, and **`get_settings()`** returns a fresh instance. The variables you'll touch most:

- **`ONBOARDING_LLM_BACKEND`**: only `claude_sdk` is supported. Set **`CLAUDE_SDK_MODEL`** to pick a model, or leave it blank for the subscription's default.
- **`ONBOARDING_API_KEYS`**: comma-separated bearer keys, default `dev-local-key`. Leaving it blank turns auth off. Related limits are **`ONBOARDING_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN`** (default 60) and **`ONBOARDING_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES`** (default 16384).
- **`ONBOARDING_ALLOWED_ROOTS`**: comma-separated folders Cortex is allowed to read.
- **`ONBOARDING_VECTOR_BACKEND`**: `tfidf` (the default), `dense` or `hybrid`. Related: **`ONBOARDING_INDEX_DIR`** (default `.kt_index`), plus chunk and file-size caps such as **`ONBOARDING_MAX_INGEST_FILES`**.
- **`ONBOARDING_CHAT_STORE`**: `auto`, `json` or `mongo`. Related: **`ONBOARDING_MONGO_URI`** and **`ONBOARDING_MONGO_DB`**.
- **`ONBOARDING_MAX_RETRIES`**, **`ONBOARDING_LOG_LEVEL`** and **`ONBOARDING_TRACE_FILE`**.
- **`ONBOARDING_CLONE_INTERACTIVE`**: set it to false on headless servers so a private clone without a token fails fast. **`ONBOARDING_BITBUCKET_TOKEN`** lets Re-sync re-clone private repos.
- **`ONBOARDING_DISABLE_TRUSTSTORE`**: TLS trust is handled in `cortex/_tls.py`, which `cortex/__init__.py` imports. The README says Cortex verifies certificates against the operating system's trust store so it works behind corporate proxies, and `.env.example` says `1` disables that. When I read `_tls.py`, though, the check looked inverted: as indexed, the line that switches on the OS trust store runs only when this variable is set to `1`. I only saw a fragment of the file, so open `cortex/_tls.py` before relying on either behavior.

**CLI.** `cli/main.py` is a Typer app and prints every result as JSON:

- `python -m cli.main ingest --repo <path> -n <name> [--rebuild]` indexes a repo.
- `python -m cli.main ask "<question>" -n <name>` asks a question about an indexed repo.
- `python -m cli.main namespaces` lists indexed repos.
- `python -m cli.main info` shows the agent ID, version, backend and model.

The CLI switches stdout to UTF-8 so Windows consoles don't crash on Unicode in code snippets. It exits with code 2 on errors such as a bad path.

**Tests.** Run `.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest -q`. The suite never calls Claude, so it needs no login. To measure the real agent's answer quality, run `python -m evals.ragas_eval` or `python -m evals.repoqa_eval`. These use your Claude login.
takeaways: Keep ANTHROPIC_API_KEY unset; Cortex refuses to start otherwise (it would bill the API).
Log in once with `claude setup-token`, then run `uvicorn api.server:app --port 8000`.
All config is ONBOARDING_* env vars read by Settings in cortex/config.py (.env works).
